title: The Black Dot
guided: Sit comfortably and look toward a small, dark point.
Blink normally; when attention moves away, return gently.
Stop when your eyes become uncomfortable.
history: Atkinson describes sustained observation of an inked dot, later moving it to either side and increasing time. His original protocol discouraged blinking; the modern mode does not.
notice: Optional gentle gaze exercise. Do not stare without blinking or strain your eyes.

title: Mirror Observation
guided: Look at your reflection comfortably.
Notice changes in facial expression without judging them.
Blink as needed and rest when ready.
history: Atkinson asks readers to observe their own eyes in a mirror and gradually extend the practice.
notice: Do not force fixed staring.

title: Comfortable Stillness
guided: Sit in a supported, relaxed position.
Observe natural movements and breathing.
Experiment with gentle stillness without suppressing necessary movement.
history: Atkinson describes seated stillness practiced for five minutes and eventually longer periods.
notice: Movement and adjustments are always allowed.

title: Steady Hand
guided: Hold a lightweight, unbreakable cup partially filled with water.
Observe the movement of its surface without demanding perfect stillness.
Rest the arm as soon as it becomes uncomfortable.
history: The original exercise uses a glass filled to the brim and an outstretched arm; the adapted mode lowers spill and strain risks.
notice: Avoid heavy or breakable containers.

variations: Choose another ordinary object, such as a spoon or key; use the same observation steps.
title: Explore an Ordinary Object
guided: Choose an everyday object.
Study its form, texture, materials and possible history.
When attention wanders, return to the object.
history: Atkinson describes closely observing a pencil and considering its properties and manufacture.
notice: An observation exercise, not a clinical intervention.

title: Mental Rapport Visualization
guided: Settle comfortably and allow breathing to be natural.
Bring to mind a person who has agreed to participate in the practice.
Visualize a calm conversation, an imagined connecting corridor, and a kind intention.
Record the experience without assuming the other person perceived it.
history: Atkinson describes relaxation, the imagined image of a person and a long mental tube as a method of telepathic contact.
notice: Historical exploratory practice; telepathic communication is not scientifically established. No claims of covert influence.

title: Sequential Finger Attention
guided: Rest your hands comfortably on a table, palms up.
Gently unfold the thumb and then each finger in sequence.
Refold them in reverse order, noticing each movement.
Repeat only as comfortably as you wish; use one hand or mental rehearsal instead.
history: In Lesson XIV's movement group, Atkinson describes extending fingers one by one from a closed hand, then reversing the sequence, using both hands and gradually increasing repetition. The historical passage mentions five cycles and later ten.
notice: Do not force fingers or grip through pain. This is optional movement practice.

title: Attentive Thumb Circles
guided: Rest your hands comfortably and interlace fingers if that feels natural.
Turn the thumbs around one another slowly.
Observe the movement; change pace or stop whenever needed.
history: Atkinson describes slowly rotating the thumbs with the fingers interlaced while attending to the movement.
notice: If repetitive hand motion is uncomfortable, imagine the movement or choose another exercise.

variations: Use another comfortable finger, or imagine the movement while keeping your hand supported.
title: Deliberate Finger Movement
guided: Place one hand comfortably on your knee or a surface.
Move the index finger gently from side to side.
Notice the starting, stopping and direction of the movement.
history: Atkinson describes attending to a slow side-to-side motion of the extended index finger.
notice: Use a pain-free range; no movement is mandatory.

title: Thought Absorption and Imagery
guided: Choose a comfortable, quiet place and relax without controlling your breath.
Select a personal quality you want to explore, such as courage or patience.
Reflect on what that quality means to you.
Imagine an everyday scene in which you express that quality.
Gently return attention when distracted; finish by noting one practical action.
history: Lesson XII gives a six-stage practice: seek quiet, relax, direct attention inward, consider a quality or word such as fearlessness, imagine oneself embodying it and repeat practice. The historical source also recommends deep breathing and breath retention; these are not part of guided mode.
notice: Use natural breathing without holding your breath. This is reflective imagery, not a mental-health treatment or guaranteed personality change.

title: Gentle Arm Observation
guided: Choose a comfortable seated position.
Optionally raise one arm for a short period, or keep it supported.
Observe the fingers without straining; lower the arm whenever you wish.
history: The original exercise involves extending an arm and observing the fingers, with progressively longer periods.
notice: Skip or adapt this exercise for pain, weakness, dizziness or fatigue. Never force the arm position.

title: Movement Awareness
guided: Sit or stand in any comfortable position.
Notice small habitual movements without judging them.
Optionally choose one movement to perform more deliberately.
Allow fidgeting and necessary adjustments; reflect on what you noticed.
history: Atkinson encourages deliberate awareness and reduction of habitual restless movements as a concentration exercise.
notice: Fidgeting can be a valid self-regulation strategy. This practice does not require stopping it.

title: Fixed Mark, Gentle Head Motion
guided: Choose a comfortable mark at eye level.
Keep it in view while optionally turning your head very slightly and slowly.
Return to center and rest whenever needed.
history: Atkinson describes holding attention on a stationary mark while turning the head.
notice: Stop immediately if dizzy or visually uncomfortable. Keep your head still instead if preferred.

title: Attentive Gaze Shifting
guided: Choose two or three comfortable points around the room.
Move your attention slowly between points, blinking normally.
Rest your gaze or finish at the first sign of strain.
history: Atkinson describes shifting gaze among points in different directions and stopping when tired.
notice: Natural blinking, pauses, and a static alternative are always allowed.

title: Mutual Gaze with Consent
guided: Invite an adult practice partner who freely agrees to take part.
Agree on a short comfortable interval and a stop signal.
Observe each other's gaze without trying to control or intimidate.
End immediately if either person wishes.
history: Atkinson describes attempts at sustained partner eye contact and speculates about interpersonal influence.
notice: Never try this on strangers or animals; do not claim hypnotic influence.

title: Imagined Turn of Attention
guided: Picture a fictional person walking ahead in a safe imagined scene.
Imagine them turning toward a sound or invitation.
Notice your image and distinguish imagination from an event outside your mind.
history: Atkinson proposes attempting to prompt a person walking ahead to turn through mental intention.
notice: A private visualization adaptation; do not target unwitting people or claim influence.

title: Imagining Attention in a Gathering
guided: Picture a fictional gathering from a comfortable perspective.
Choose a person in your imagined scene.
Imagine them noticing a consensual invitation to connect.
Describe your experience without assuming real-world effects.
history: Atkinson describes focusing on a seated individual and imagining they will turn toward the practitioner.
notice: Exploratory imagery only; no covert attention experiments.

title: Imagined Attention without Eye Contact
guided: Imagine a voluntary interaction with a person who has agreed to participate.
Form a clear mental picture of an invitation to interact.
Finish by reflecting on your expectations, not assumed outcomes.
history: Atkinson describes efforts to attract another person's attention without visible gaze.
notice: Do not treat any external response as proof of telepathy.

title: Consensual Word Imagery
guided: With a willing partner, separately select a familiar word or agree to a blinded guessing protocol.
One participant visualizes the word while the other independently records a guess.
Reveal only after recording the guess; include misses in reflection.
history: Atkinson describes silently suggesting a forgotten word to another person.
notice: A voluntary word-guessing activity, not demonstrated thought transmission. No live paired server is connected.

title: Imagined Direction and Choice
guided: Imagine a fictional character standing at a fork in a road.
Visualize a possible direction they could choose.
Record the imagined choice and notice uncertainty.
history: Atkinson proposes mentally influencing the walking direction of another person.
notice: Only fictional visualization here; do not interfere with real pedestrians.

title: Window Scene Visualization
guided: Imagine observing a peaceful street from a window.
Picture a fictional passerby noticing something interesting nearby.
Allow the scene to fade and record what you imagined.
history: Atkinson proposes attempting to make a passerby look toward the practitioner from a window.
notice: Do not target real strangers; imagery is not evidence of external influence.

title: Quiet Preparation for Mental Imagery
guided: Find a comfortable position in a quiet environment.
Let the shoulders soften and breathe naturally.
Notice the mind settling, without forcing thoughts away.
history: Atkinson begins the telepathic-will practice by inviting the reader to relax in a quiet place.
notice: Stop when uncomfortable. This practice is not a treatment.

title: Imagining a Familiar Person
guided: Choose a person who has agreed to be included in this exercise, or invent a fictional character.
Imagine their appearance and familiar context gently.
Notice when the image becomes clearer or less distinct without attaching a supernatural explanation.
history: Atkinson advises forming a vivid image of the intended recipient of a thought.
notice: Vivid imagery does not establish communication or consent to contact.

title: Imagined Conversation
guided: Imagine a friendly, voluntary conversation.
Form a simple message and visualize speaking it.
Reflect on the experience as an internal visualization, not confirmation of receipt.
history: Atkinson describes mentally addressing an intended person and imagining a response.
notice: No claim of actual remote message transmission.

title: Affirming Personal Agency
guided: Sit or stand comfortably.
Consider a grounded phrase such as 'I can choose my next action.'
Recall a simple choice you can make today.
Finish by identifying one practical step.
history: Atkinson discusses an 'I am' affirmation as a means of protecting the mind against imagined influence.
notice: A reflective agency exercise; this does not validate claims of outside mental control.

title: The Mental Castle
guided: Sit alone somewhere quiet, away from conversation or pressure to decide quickly.
Bring back the 'I am' affirmation, picturing your own steady presence.
Surround that image with calm, supportive thoughts, like walls around a quiet room.
From inside that steadiness, consider the question or pressure you are facing, then decide on your own terms.
history: Atkinson extends the 'I am' affirmation into a defensive practice: picturing oneself inside a protective 'mental castle' of supportive thoughts in order to think clearly when swayed by others' opinions or crowd feeling.
notice: A grounding practice for clearer thinking under social pressure; it is not a scientifically established defense against outside mental influence and does not replace sound judgment or professional support.

title: Everyday Task Focus
guided: Choose one small everyday task, such as reading a paragraph or organizing a few items.
Decide what a useful next step would be and reduce optional distractions.
Work on that step; when attention wanders, gently return. Movement and breaks are welcome.
Finish by noting what you did and one thing that helped your attention.
history: Lesson XIII recommends concentrating attention on one task at a time and applying concentration to everyday work. This timed session and reflection sequence are a modern adaptation, not a numbered exercise from the book. The five-minute duration is an app default, not a historical prescription.
notice: Modern adaptation of Lesson XIII. Adjust the duration and take breaks; no productivity or health outcome is guaranteed.
durationProvenance: App-selected default; adjust or stop at any time. Not a duration prescribed in the source.

title: Attentive Listening
guided: Choose a short recording or invite a willing partner to share something for a comfortable interval.
Listen to the words and meaning. Eye contact is optional; use captions or a transcript if helpful.
When distracted, return gently without judging yourself.
At a natural pause, summarize what you understood. With a partner, ask whether you understood correctly and respect their wish to stop.
history: Lesson V discusses the art of listening and illustrates it with an anecdote about Thomas Carlyle. The recording option, summary, consent guidance and three-minute duration are modern additions. This practice does not adopt the chapter's persuasion claims.
notice: Modern adaptation of Lesson V. No recording or messages are sent by the app. Use a transcript or quiet solo reflection if preferred.
durationProvenance: App-selected default; adjust or stop at any time. Not a duration prescribed in the source.

title: One Small Habit Action
guided: Choose a personally meaningful habit you want to practice, without labeling yourself as good or bad.
Pick one small action within your control, such as opening a book or preparing tomorrow's materials.
Choose a familiar moment when you could try that action. Make it smaller if needed.
Try it now if practical, or note your next opportunity. Reflect on what helped without treating a missed attempt as failure.
history: Lesson XII discusses acquired habits and developing personal qualities. The small-action plan, familiar cue and reflection are a proposed modern practice inspired by that discussion, not Atkinson's original protocol. The three-minute duration is an app default; no historical or clinical efficacy claim is made.
notice: Modern practice inspired by Lesson XII. Optional personal reflection, not treatment or a promise of character change.
durationProvenance: App-selected default; adjust or stop at any time. Not a duration prescribed in the source.
